name: Magnolia Mother's Trust
eligibility: Low-income Black mothers in Jackson; the first cohort was limited to working Black mothers in subsidized housing, chosen by lottery
operator: Springboard to Opportunities, a Jackson nonprofit, funded by private donors; it launched with $300,000 from the Economic Security Project and a private donor
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 12 months to low-income Black mothers in Jackson, plus $1,000 into a college savings account per child; it began in 2018 with 20 mothers, and over 550 mothers have been paid across six cohorts
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Baby's First Years
city: New York City, New Orleans, Twin Cities, Omaha
eligibility: Mothers with incomes below the federal poverty line, recruited at hospitals around their child's birth (May 2018–June 2019); randomly assigned to $333 or $20 a month
place: New York City, New Orleans, the Twin Cities and Omaha, USA
operator: A university research team funded by the National Institutes of Health and private foundations, with payments on a debit card
paid: $333 a month with no conditions, from the child's birth until three months after their sixth birthday (76 months), to low-income mothers in four US metro areas; 1,000 mothers recruited in 2018–2019 were randomly assigned to $333 or to $20 a month
result: The researchers (NBER working paper, May 2025) reported no statistically significant effects at age four on language, executive function, social-emotional problems or brain activity, vs the $20 group (n = 891 children), and none on three secondary outcomes; they say effects may still appear later
evaluation.by: Noble, Magnuson, Duncan, Gennetian, Yoshikawa et al.

name: Stockton Economic Empowerment Demonstration (SEED)
eligibility: Stockton residents 18+ living in census tracts at or below the city's median household income ($46,033); about 4,200 households were mailed invitations, 478 applied, and recipients were picked at random
operator: Stockton Economic Empowerment Demonstration (SEED), started by then-Mayor Michael Tubbs and paid for by private donors and foundations, not the city budget
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months (February 2019–January 2021) to 125 randomly selected residents of Stockton's lower-income neighborhoods (the study assigned 131 people to receive it and 200 to a control group)
result: A peer-reviewed randomized trial (Journal of Urban Health, 2023; 131 treatment, 200 control) reported lower income volatility (19% vs 26%), less psychological distress and better energy and physical functioning than the control group in the first year. Most gaps were no longer significant in the second, pandemic year, and employment differences were not significant
evaluation.by: Stacia West (University of Tennessee) and Amy Castro (University of Pennsylvania)

name: HudsonUP Basic Income Pilot
eligibility: Hudson residents earning less than the area median income, chosen by randomized lottery in three cohorts: 25 adults from fall 2020 (paid 2020–2025), 50 from 2021 (2021–2026) and 53 from 2022 (2022–2027)
operator: HudsonUP, a privately funded pilot in the small city of Hudson, started by The Spark of Hudson and Andrew Yang's Humanity Forward, with research by the Jain Family Institute
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for five years to 128 low-income residents (about 2% of the city) chosen by lottery in three cohorts: 25 from fall 2020, 50 from 2021 and 53 from 2022, the last of whom are paid until 2027
result: The Jain Family Institute's final report (February 2026), based on surveys and interviews with no comparison group, said the cash eased day-to-day stress but a majority still could not cover a $400 emergency (first cohort: 62.5% by summer 2025), and 8–24% moved in any six-month period. Survey response rates averaged 25%
evaluation.by: Jain Family Institute (Leah Hamilton, with Appalachian State University)

name: Santa Clara County Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot for Transition-Age Foster Youth
eligibility: Young adults aged 21–24 who had been in the county's foster care system, some still receiving support services
operator: Santa Clara County government, with the Gerald Huff Fund for Humanity, a basic income nonprofit
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 12 months (June 2020–May 2021) to 72 young adults aged 21–24 leaving foster care, described as the first such program in the US
result: No published evaluation yet

name: People's Prosperity Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Families in CollegeBound Saint Paul (the city's children's savings account program) at or under 300% of the poverty line who self-attested to COVID-19 hardship; randomly selected
operator: City of Saint Paul under Mayor Melvin Carter, the first Mayors for a Guaranteed Income pilot, paid mostly from philanthropy with some federal CARES Act and state money
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months (October 2020–April 2022) to 150 low-income Saint Paul families, plus $10 a month into each child's college savings account
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (December 2023) reported employment among recipients rising from 49% at the start to 63% six months after payments ended, and the share with high hope rising from 15% to 22%; financial well-being fell back after the cash ended. These are before-and-after changes for recipients only, not a comparison with a control group
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Richmond Resilience Initiative
eligibility: Richmond residents in the city's workforce program with children under 18, employed but earning too much for federal benefits yet less than a living wage (the 'cliff effect'); the third cohort was for people returning from prison
operator: City of Richmond's Office of Community Wealth Building under Mayor Levar Stoney, paid from foundation money and later federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months to 94 working parents in several cohorts between October 2020 and May 2025, aimed at people who had lost public benefits but did not yet earn a living wage
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research on the first cohort of 18 (May 2024), comparing before and after: average monthly savings rose from $147 to $305 and the share unable to cover a $400 emergency fell from 59% to 20%. Very small sample, no control group reported
evaluation.by: Penn Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Chelsea Eats
eligibility: Low-income Chelsea households, many hit by COVID-19 job losses and recruited largely from food pantry users; cards allocated by lottery
operator: City of Chelsea, paid from federal COVID relief, state and philanthropic money (including the Shah Family Foundation), studied by Harvard researchers
paid: $200–$400 a month (by household size) with no conditions on a debit card for nine months (November 2020–August 2021) to about 2,000 low-income households, roughly 15% of the city's households, chosen by lottery
result: Harvard researchers (JAMA, 2024), comparing lottery winners with non-winners using hospital records: 27% fewer emergency department visits, including 62% fewer for behavioral health and 87% fewer related to substance use, and 42% fewer hospital admissions from the ED; no short-term change in blood pressure, weight or cholesterol
evaluation.by: Sumit Agarwal, Benjamin Lê Cook and Jeffrey Liebman (Harvard)

name: OpenResearch Unconditional Cash Study
eligibility: Adults aged 21–40 with household income at or below 300% of the federal poverty level, in 19 urban, suburban and rural counties of Illinois and Texas; randomized in October 2020 after enrollment from August 2019 to October 2020
operator: OpenResearch, a nonprofit research lab, with economists including Eva Vivalt, Elizabeth Rhodes, Alexander Bartik, David Broockman, Patrick Krause and Sarah Miller
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for three years (November 2020–October 2023) to 1,000 low-income people aged 21–40 in 19 counties of Illinois and Texas; 2,000 others were randomly assigned to a control group that got $50 a month
result: The researchers (NBER working paper, July 2024; published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026) reported, vs the control group: income excluding the transfers fell by about $1,900 a year, recipients worked 1–2 fewer hours a week, mostly taking more leisure, and spending rose broadly; there was no measurable gain in job quality, and higher well-being in year one faded afterward
evaluation.by: Vivalt, Rhodes, Bartik, Broockman, Krause and Miller (OpenResearch)

name: Newark Movement for Economic Equity
eligibility: Newark residents 18+ with income at or below 200% of the federal poverty line and hurt by COVID-19, chosen at random; 478 others formed a control group
operator: City of Newark under Mayor Ras Baraka, with Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, paid from $6.2 million of private and public money including federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $6,000 a year with no conditions for two years to 400 low-income residents hit by COVID-19, half as $250 every two weeks and half as $3,000 every six months; payments began with 30 people in summer 2021
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (June 2025), compared with 478 controls, reported that the every-two-weeks payments reduced income swings and improved food security and rent payment, while lump-sum recipients more often reported savings over $500; the summary gives no effect sizes
evaluation.by: Penn Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Dallas guaranteed income eviction-prevention pilot (United Way of Metropolitan Dallas)
eligibility: Vulnerable residents in Dallas communities with high eviction-filing rates and schools with high student mobility; average income about $14,000 a year
operator: United Way of Metropolitan Dallas with community partners, paid from philanthropic money with no city funds
paid: $250 a month with no conditions for up to three years from fall 2021 to 500 low-income Dallas residents in areas with high eviction rates (about a 23% boost to their average income of $14,000)
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Compton Pledge
eligibility: Low-income Compton residents (below twice the federal poverty line), including undocumented and formerly incarcerated residents; picked by lottery
operator: Fund for Guaranteed Income, a charity backed by private donors and family foundations, with the City of Compton and the Jain Family Institute; no city money
paid: An average of about $500 a month with no conditions for two years (February 2021–April 2023) to about 800 low-income households, with amounts varying by family size; half were paid twice a month and half once a quarter
result: An NBER working paper (2024, not peer-reviewed) compared 695 recipient households with 1,402 controls: no significant change in work for full-time workers, but labor force participation fell 13 points among part-time workers; recipients reported lower earned income and spent $302 a month less; housing security improved; twice-monthly payments beat quarterly on food security and credit card debt
evaluation.by: Balakrishnan, Chan, Constantino, Haushofer and Morduch (Jain Family Institute, NYU, Stanford, Stockholm University), NBER working paper w33209

name: SF Guaranteed Income Pilot for Artists (SF-GIPA)
eligibility: San Francisco artists disproportionately impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic
operator: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts (YBCA), a San Francisco arts center, in partnership with the City of San Francisco and with support from private donors
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 130 San Francisco artists hit by the pandemic ($2.34 million in total), launched in May 2021
result: No published evaluation yet

name: MOMentum (Marin Guaranteed Income Demonstration Project)
eligibility: Low-income Black, Indigenous and other mothers of color in Marin County with at least one child under 18
operator: Marin Community Foundation, a private foundation, with the nonprofit UpTogether running the payments
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for two years from May 2021 to 125 low-income mothers of color in Marin County, followed by a third year of tapering payments that ended in May 2024
result: Social Policy Research Associates (February 2024) reported from a self-reported survey (68% of 122 mothers) and 30 interviews: stable housing rose from 45% to 60%, 76% said debt was more manageable and 59% said their health improved. There was no control group
evaluation.by: Social Policy Research Associates

name: Guaranteed Income Validation Effort (GIVE)
eligibility: Gary residents 18+ earning $35,000 a year or less; chosen by lottery
operator: City of Gary's Guaranteed Income Validation Effort, started with $500,000 from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income (funded partly by Jack Dorsey)
paid: $500 a month with no strings attached for 12 months from May 2021 to 125 residents earning $35,000 a year or less, chosen by lottery
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Project Resilience
eligibility: Ulster County households with annual income at or below $46,900 (80% of area median income), chosen by lottery; 84 others formed a control group
operator: Ulster County government, described as the first county-led guaranteed income program in the US, paid from private donations with Community Foundations of the Hudson Valley and Ulster Savings Bank
paid: $500 a month with no conditions to 100 low-income households (income at or below $46,900) from May 2021, extended from 12 to 17 months with a phase-out to $250 by September 2022
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (November 2023), compared with 84 control households, reported higher household income and savings, a better ability to handle financial emergencies, and better physical and mental health and housing stability; the summary gives no effect sizes
evaluation.by: Penn Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Abundant Birth Project
eligibility: Black and/or Pasifika pregnant people living in San Francisco (or moved out within six months), under 27 weeks pregnant, household income under $100,000; picked in bimonthly random 'Abundance Drawings'
operator: Expecting Justice, a San Francisco birth justice collaborative, with the city's Department of Public Health and a citywide group of public and private partners
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions, from pregnancy to about six months after birth (up to 14 months), to 151 Black and Pacific Islander pregnant people in San Francisco chosen by lottery; launched on Juneteenth 2021 and ended in January 2024
result: A peer-reviewed acceptability study (BMC Public Health, 2026; 116 surveyed, 21 interviewed) reported that 95.7% were very satisfied and 77.5% trusted the program to act in their interest, vs 9% for government. It did not measure birth outcomes and had no control group
evaluation.by: UCSF California Preterm Birth Initiative and community researchers

name: The Bridge Project
eligibility: Low-income pregnant women and new mothers (first-time mothers from 2022) in Washington Heights, Inwood and Harlem, later also the Bronx; undocumented residents eligible
place: New York City, New York, USA
operator: The Bridge Project, New York City's first guaranteed income program, run and funded privately by the Monarch Foundation to cover a child's first 1,000 days
paid: Up to $1,000 a month with no conditions for three years to low-income mothers, from 100 mothers in northern Manhattan in June 2021 to about 600 by summer 2022 (an extra 500 first-time mothers from April 2022)
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Oakland Resilient Families
eligibility: Families with at least one child under 18. Cohort 1: residents of a one-square-mile area of East Oakland with income below 50% of Area Median Income. Cohort 2: Oakland households below 138% of the federal poverty level. Chosen by two lotteries, one per phase
operator: City of Oakland (Mayor Libby Schaaf's office) with the nonprofits UpTogether and Oakland Thrives, paid entirely from philanthropic donations
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 600 low-income Oakland families with children, chosen by lottery in two cohorts; payments ran July 2021–June 2023
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (April 2025) reported that full-time employment rose faster among recipients (15% to 26%) than in the control group (14% to 18%) and that recipients' income stayed more stable. The authors said the amount allowed only temporary respite in a rapidly gentrifying city
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research (Flynn, Tandon, Nichols, Thompson, West and Castro)

name: Direct Investment Program in Sacramento (DIPS)
eligibility: Low-income Sacramento County households (income limits shown in the program's 2021–2023 eligibility chart; details not read)
operator: United Way California Capital Region, a regional charity, with the nonprofit UpTogether
paid: $300 a month with no conditions for two years (2021–June 2023) to 100 low-income households in Sacramento County, the region's first guaranteed income program
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Cambridge RISE (Recurring Income for Success and Empowerment)
eligibility: Cambridge single caregivers 18+ with at least one child under 18 and income below 80% of area median income, chosen at random; 156 others formed a control group
operator: Cambridge Community Foundation and then-Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, paid entirely from private money (including Harvard and MIT), with a randomized study by Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months from September 2021 to 130 low-income single caregivers chosen at random
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (March 2024), compared with 156 controls: full-time employment rose from 36% to 40% among recipients while it fell from 30% to 28% in the control group; recipients also had higher incomes, less income volatility and better food security
evaluation.by: Penn Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Arlington's Guarantee
eligibility: Arlington households with children under 18 earning about 30% of area median income (under about $46,600), chosen at random, including 25 undocumented households and 25 people returning from incarceration
operator: Arlington Community Foundation, paid from $2 million of private donations, with the county's Department of Human Services
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 200 very low-income households with children, chosen at random, with payments between September 2021 and late 2023
result: The Arlington Community Foundation and county human services (February 2024) reported recipients' monthly work income rose 36% ($1,200 to $1,640) vs 9% for a control group, and employment rose from 75% to 87%. Not an independent evaluation; most still could not cover a $400 emergency
evaluation.by: Arlington Community Foundation and Arlington County Department of Human Services

name: Columbia Life Improvement Monetary Boost (CLIMB)
eligibility: Fathers aged 18+ in Columbia (ZIP codes 29203 and 29223) who were current or former clients of the Midlands Fatherhood Coalition; randomly selected
operator: City of Columbia with the Midlands Fatherhood Coalition, paid entirely from private and philanthropic money ($600,000), including Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (September 2021–August 2022) to 100 low-income fathers chosen at random; 130 others formed a control group
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (February 2024), vs 130 controls: recipients kept full-time jobs at higher rates, had better food security and less income volatility, and spent mostly on their children; but they reported higher stress throughout, and many owed about $300 a month in child support
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Santa Fe LEAP (Learn, Earn, Achieve Program)
eligibility: Santa Fe Community College students aged 30 or under in its Expanding Opportunities for Young Families program, primary caretakers of at least one child under 18, income below 200% of the federal poverty line; picked by random selection
operator: The City of Santa Fe under Mayor Alan Webber, with Santa Fe Community College, the Santa Fe Community Foundation and Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $400 a month with no conditions for a year (October 2021–September 2022) to 100 Santa Fe Community College students aged 30 or under raising children, picked at random from eligible students
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research reported (as summarized by the college, 2025) that participants' median annual income rose from $19,500 to $24,000, full-time employment rose 19 points and about 30% graduated during or soon after the program; these are before-and-after figures without a comparison group
evaluation.by: Center for Guaranteed Income Research, University of Pennsylvania

name: South San Francisco Guaranteed Income Pilot Program
eligibility: Low-income South San Francisco households (all below 30% of Area Median Income), prioritising families at risk of displacement, foster youth, families with young children and the lowest-income neighborhoods; undocumented residents eligible
operator: City of South San Francisco, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA) and a county grant; the YMCA Community Resource Center ran it
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months, from November 2021, to 160 low-income households (with 275 children), plus optional budgeting and financial counselling
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Providence Guaranteed Income Program
eligibility: Providence residents 18+ with income below 200% of the federal poverty level, chosen by a lottery weighted to reflect the city's population in poverty; a control group took part in surveys
operator: City of Providence under Mayor Jorge Elorza, paid from private donations (including $500,000 from Jack Dorsey) and then federal pandemic relief (ARPA), with Amos House as lead agency
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months (November 2021–April 2023, extended from 12) to 110 low-income residents chosen by lottery
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Growing Resilience in Tacoma (GRIT)
eligibility: Employed single-income households with children under 17 (or with disabilities up to 21), income 100%–200% of the federal poverty level, living in the Eastside, Hilltop, South Tacoma or South End neighborhoods; chosen at random from over 2,000 applicants
operator: United Way of Pierce County and the City of Tacoma, launched by Mayor Victoria Woodards, with money from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income and other public and private funders
paid: $500 a month with no conditions from December 2021 to December 2022 to 110 working single-earner families with children in four Tacoma neighborhoods, chosen at random from over 2,000 applicants
result: No published evaluation yet

name: TAYportunity Guaranteed Income
eligibility: Young adults 18–24 on General Relief and in the county's START/TAYportunity employment program, not in another GI program; applications May 23–June 6, 2022; picked by lottery
operator: Los Angeles County Department of Public Social Services (DPSS), a county program, not the city's
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 36 months from 2022 to 300 young adults aged 18–24 on the county's General Relief aid, picked by lottery, with optional paid job training; 650 others formed the control group
result: A University of Virginia economist's job market paper (2025, not peer-reviewed), comparing 300 recipients with 566 controls, reported employment up 7 percentage points (18%), monthly earnings up about $94 (30%), felony arrests down 40% and births down by nearly half; estimates using caseworker assignment suggest job training, on top of the cash, drove much of the job gains
evaluation.by: Marcella Cartledge, University of Virginia (job market paper, 'The Effects of Cash-Plus Programs on Young Adults: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment in Los Angeles County')

name: CollegeBound Boost
eligibility: Saint Paul parents or guardians of a CollegeBound child (born to a Saint Paul resident on or after 1 January 2020), household income at or below 300% of the federal poverty level; randomly assigned
operator: City of Saint Paul, paid from $4 million of federal pandemic relief (ARPA) and $1 million of philanthropy; the University of Michigan is studying it
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for two years plus $1,000 in the child's college savings account to 333 low-income families with young children, randomly selected from 2022; other groups got the $1,000 only or neither
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot (Workforce Development Council of Seattle-King County)
eligibility: Low-income people including students and justice-involved adults (88% BIPOC, 58% women), paired with case management, career planning and financial education
place: Seattle and King County, Washington, USA
operator: The Workforce Development Council of Seattle-King County, a workforce agency, funded by Washington State's Employment Security Department, King County and Chase Bank
paid: $500 a month for 10 months, starting in fall 2022, to 102 low-income people in King County, alongside case management, career planning and financial education
result: An evaluation by Applied Inference (March 2024) reported employment among participants rising from 37% to 66% and the savings rate among families with children from 0% to 42%; these are before-and-after figures with no control group, and the payments came with job services
evaluation.by: Applied Inference

name: New Mexico Immigrant Guaranteed Basic Income Project
eligibility: Undocumented and mixed-immigration-status families, many shut out of pandemic stimulus and unemployment aid; about one-third rural and two-thirds urban; applications closed 11 February 2022
operator: A coalition of New Mexico immigrant and policy groups (the NM Economic Relief Working Group) with the nonprofit UpTogether, funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation and UpTogether
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months, from 2022, to 330 undocumented and mixed-immigration-status families across New Mexico who had been left out of most pandemic aid
result: The working group's report (December 2023) reported a 35% drop in trouble paying rent or mortgage on time and a 14% rise in employment among rural participants; it is self-reported, with no control group, and was published by the groups that ran the program
evaluation.by: NM Economic Relief Working Group

name: BIG:LEAP (Basic Income Guaranteed: Los Angeles Economic Assistance Pilot)
eligibility: City of Los Angeles residents 18+, income below the federal poverty line, with a dependent child (or a student under 24) or pregnant, and financially or medically hit by COVID-19; picked at random from more than 50,000 applicants
place: City of Los Angeles, California, USA
operator: City of Los Angeles (Community Investment for Families Department), paid from the city's general fund and council district funds
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 12 months (payments January 2022–March 2023) to 3,202 households below the poverty line with a child or a pregnancy and hit by COVID-19; more than 50,000 applied, and 4,992 others formed a control group
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (July 2024), with UCLA, compared recipients with 4,992 controls and reported a significantly greater ability to cover a $400 emergency, less food insecurity, more time for parenting and less severe and less frequent partner violence; LAist reported the share able to cover a $400 emergency rose from about 10% to about 15% among recipients
evaluation.by: Center for Guaranteed Income Research, University of Pennsylvania (with UCLA Fielding School of Public Health)

name: Income Mobility Program for Atlanta Community Transformation (I.M.P.A.C.T.)
eligibility: Atlanta residents aged 18+ with household income at or below 200% of the 2021 federal poverty guidelines; 275 in an evaluated cohort and 25 in a storytelling cohort
operator: Urban League of Greater Atlanta with the City of Atlanta, funded by $2 million from the city (developer money from Centennial Yards) and $500,000 from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (payments January 2022–May 2023) to 300 Atlanta residents at or below 200% of the poverty line
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Just Income GNV
eligibility: Alachua County residents with a felony conviction released from state or federal prison or a Florida county jail within the past six months
operator: Community Spring, a Gainesville nonprofit led by formerly incarcerated people, funded privately by Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, Spring Point Partners and donors
paid: $1,000 in the first month and then $600 a month with no conditions for a year to 115 people recently released from incarceration with felony convictions, in two cohorts starting January and March 2022
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (February 2025), vs a control group, reported that recipients were better able to cover emergencies, saved more, had more stable housing, better food security and mental health, and lower recidivism; the summaries gave no figures, and the sample was about 100 people
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research (with Lucius Couloute)

name: Financial Assistance for Phoenix Families
eligibility: Phoenix households at or below 80% of area median income ($63,200 for a family of four) who had applied for emergency rental assistance or lived in city public housing or used Section 8 vouchers; chosen by lottery from about 7,000 eligible families
operator: The City of Phoenix, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $1,000 a month for 12 months in 2022 on prepaid debit cards to 1,000 low-income Phoenix families chosen by lottery from about 7,000 eligible; the card could not be used for alcohol, tobacco or lottery tickets
result: No published evaluation yet

name: San Diego for Every Child Guaranteed Income Project
eligibility: Adults 18+ with a child 12 or younger, living in ZIP codes 92114 (Encanto), 92139 (Paradise Hills), 91950 (National City) or 92173 (San Ysidro), income up to $53,000 for a family of four; picked at random (about 3,500 others also applied); no work or citizenship requirement
place: San Diego and National City, California, USA
operator: Jewish Family Service of San Diego with the City of San Diego and National City, paid from state money and the Alliance Healthcare Foundation
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months (March 2022–February 2024) to 150 families with a child aged 12 or younger in four high-poverty ZIP codes, picked at random
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Embrace Mothers
eligibility: Female-identifying single heads of family aged 18+ with children under 18 (including grandmothers and aunts in a mothering role), living in Birmingham; randomly selected by Abt Global; more than 8,000 mothers applied
operator: City of Birmingham, funded with $495,000 from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income; Abt Global ran the randomized evaluation
paid: $375 a month with no conditions for 12 months (March 2022–February 2023) to 110 households led by single mothers, picked at random from more than 8,000 applicants; 132 other single mothers formed a control group
result: Abt Global's randomized evaluation (August 2024), vs 132 controls, reported that recipients had less utility debt, were better able to cover a $400 emergency and saved more, and that mothers who kept working had significantly fewer work problems caused by childcare; survey results, small sample
evaluation.by: Abt Global (for Mayors for a Guaranteed Income)

name: Shreveport Guaranteed Income Program (SGIP)
eligibility: Single parents or guardians (not living with a romantic partner) in Shreveport/Caddo Parish with household income at or below 120% of the federal poverty level; random selection weighted so about half came from lower-income areas
operator: City of Shreveport with United Way of Northwest Louisiana (Shreveport Financial Empowerment Center), paid from private donations for six months and Caddo Parish Commission money for six; part of Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $660 a month with no conditions for 12 months (March 2022–February 2023) to 110 families led by single parents at or below 120% of the poverty line, chosen at random; 132 others formed a control group
result: Abt Global's randomized evaluation (October 2024), vs 132 controls: 25% of parents could cover a $400 emergency vs 13%, and 58% were food secure at the end vs 36%; no effect on employment. Most gains lasted only while payments continued, and six months after they ended some outcomes were worse than the control group's
evaluation.by: Abt Global (for Mayors for a Guaranteed Income)

name: Excel (StepUp Durham guaranteed income pilot)
eligibility: People released from incarceration within the past five years, returning to Durham, with income at or below 60% of the area median income
operator: StepUp Durham with the City of Durham, paid mostly from a donation by Jack Dorsey plus other private donors
paid: $600 a month with no conditions for 12 months from March 2022 to 109 formerly incarcerated Durham residents
result: Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (February 2025), vs a control group: recidivism was low in both groups with no significant difference; recipients were more likely to keep full-time jobs and reported less difficulty affording food and fewer probation or parole violations
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Yolo County Basic Income (YoBI)
eligibility: Yolo County families on CalWORKs with at least one child under 6 who were homeless or unstably housed (in the county's Housing Support Program)
operator: Yolo County Health and Human Services, with UC Davis researchers
paid: About $1,289 a month on average ($1,200–$1,500, topping CalWORKs up to just above the California poverty line) with no conditions for two years (April 2022–March 2024) to 76 families with young children who were homeless or unstably housed
result: A UC Davis peer-reviewed qualitative study (2026) reported that families were lifted above the state poverty line, with better housing stability and lower stress, but for most it did not lead to lasting financial independence: one emergency could erase gains ('survival mode'). Based on participants' accounts, not a comparison group
evaluation.by: Catherine Brinkley and colleagues, UC Davis (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health)

name: New Orleans Guaranteed Income Program
eligibility: Young people aged 16–24 in Orleans Parish who were disconnected from work and school, referred by partner organizations
operator: City of New Orleans (Mayor's Office of Youth and Families), funded by a $500,000 grant from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $350 a month with no conditions for 10 months (April 2022–March 2023) to 125 young people aged 16–24 who were out of work and school
result: The city, citing Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research (August 2024), reported full-time employment among participants rose from 6% at the start to 21%, and income volatility fell by nearly 20 points; there was no control group, so changes cannot be attributed to the payments
evaluation.by: University of Pennsylvania Center for Guaranteed Income Research

name: Young Adult Louisville Income for Transformation (YALift!)
eligibility: Residents aged 18–24 in the California, Russell and Smoketown neighborhoods
operator: Metro United Way with Louisville Metro Government and Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (April 2022–March 2023) to 151 young adults aged 18–24 in three low-income Louisville neighborhoods; 180 similar residents formed a comparison group
result: Abt Global (October 2024), vs 180 non-recipients: recipients were more likely to have saved $500 or more and less likely to be evicted, both statistically significant; Metro United Way reported they were 3 times as likely to afford a $400 emergency. Higher income and work were not clearly due to the money, given the small sample
evaluation.by: Abt Global (for Mayors for a Guaranteed Income)

name: Multnomah Mothers' Trust
eligibility: Black mothers heading households with children who were already receiving services from the Black Parent Initiative or WomenFirst
operator: Multnomah County's Multnomah Idea Lab, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA), working through two community groups, the Black Parent Initiative and WomenFirst
paid: About $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months (May 2022–June 2024) to about 100 Black mothers in Multnomah County, which includes Portland, plus $50 a month for those who reported on their finances
result: An interim report by the Multnomah Idea Lab (summarized by the Oregon Center for Public Policy, 2026) reported gradual gains in income and assets, debt cut to near zero for members with deep debt, and the share at high risk of eviction falling by more than half; there was no control group
evaluation.by: Multnomah Idea Lab (Ebonee Bell, Mary Li, Steve Van Eck)

name: Breathe: LA County's Guaranteed Income Program
eligibility: Adults 18+ living in a county neighborhood at or below area median income, household income at or below AMI (single) or 120% AMI (two or more), financially hit by COVID-19, one per household; picked at random
operator: Los Angeles County (Board of Supervisors and the CEO's Poverty Alleviation Initiative); the nonprofit Strength Based Community Change ran payments by prepaid debit card
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for three years (June 2022–August 2025) to 1,000 randomly selected low-income county residents hit by COVID-19, plus 200 former foster youth for two years; about 1,200 others formed a control group
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Minneapolis Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot
eligibility: Adults 18+ in nine low-income Minneapolis ZIP codes, household income at or below 50% of area median income, affected by the pandemic; chosen at random
operator: City of Minneapolis, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA); the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis evaluated it
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months (June 2022–June 2024) to 200 low-income households in nine Minneapolis ZIP codes, chosen at random; 329 others were a control group paid $150 per survey
result: A Minneapolis Fed working paper (December 2024, randomized, 200 recipients vs 329 controls) reported that the payments improved food security, housing stability and financial security, mental health and self-reported well-being while they lasted, with no effect on work; attrition differed between groups, which the authors adjusted for
evaluation.by: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (Andrew Goodman-Bacon and Vanessa Palmer)

name: Guaranteed Income for Artists (Creatives Rebuild New York)
eligibility: Artists in New York State with financial need, picked by a weighted lottery from more than 22,000 applicants; priority groups (by race, disability, sexual orientation, citizenship status and caregiving) had better odds
operator: Creatives Rebuild New York (CRNY), an artist-support initiative funded mainly by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, with the Stavros Niarchos and Ford foundations
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 2,400 low-income artists in the state, enrolled in staggered groups from June 2022 (last payments March 2024), picked by a weighted lottery from more than 22,000 applicants
result: Indiana University researchers (Journal of Cultural Economics, accepted 2026) compared recipients with applicants not selected: about 3.9 more hours a week on arts work and 2.4 fewer on other work. Total earnings were about $11,600 a year lower, close to the $12,000 paid, but the authors say they cannot confidently attribute this to the program because artists' incomes vary so much
evaluation.by: Joanna Woronkowicz (Indiana University) and Doug Noonan (Indiana University Indianapolis)

name: Ithaca Guaranteed Income
eligibility: Ithaca residents with income at or below 80% of area median income who are primary unpaid caregivers of children or of aging or disabled adults
operator: City of Ithaca, with Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, paid from private grants from nonprofit organizations and studied by Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research
paid: $450 a month with no conditions on a prepaid card for 12 months (June 2022–May 2023) to 110 low-income unpaid caregivers of children or of older or disabled adults
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Montgomery County Boost (Guaranteed Income Pilot)
eligibility: 100 households transitioning from homelessness and 200 households with at least one child who had sought county help during COVID-19
operator: Montgomery County government (Department of Health and Human Services), paid from county funds with the Meyer Foundation and the Greater Washington Community Foundation
paid: $800 a month with no conditions for 24 months to 300 households, 100 leaving homelessness and 200 families with children, enrolled in phases from June to November 2022
result: No published evaluation yet

name: In Her Hands
eligibility: Low-income Black women with income at or below twice the federal poverty level in Atlanta's Old Fourth Ward, College Park and rural Southwest Georgia; chosen by lottery
place: Atlanta (Old Fourth Ward), College Park and rural Southwest Georgia, USA
operator: Georgia Resilience and Opportunity Fund (GRO Fund), a nonprofit, with GiveDirectly delivering the money from a $13 million privately raised budget
paid: $20,400 over two years with no conditions ($850 a month, or $4,300 up front then $700 a month) from mid-2022 to 654 low-income Black women in Atlanta's Old Fourth Ward, College Park and rural Southwest Georgia, chosen by lottery
result: A Washington University study in Health Affairs (February 2026) compared recipients with women not selected: 40% reported high or marginal food security vs 14%, with better diet quality, and the gains grew in the second year
evaluation.by: Washington University in St. Louis (Brown School), with Clark Atlanta University

name: Chicago Resilient Communities Pilot
eligibility: Chicago residents 18+, household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, negatively affected by COVID-19; chosen by lottery from more than 176,000 applicants
operator: City of Chicago (Department of Family and Support Services), paid from federal pandemic relief money in the Chicago Recovery Plan; GiveDirectly delivered the payments
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (from July 2022) to 5,000 low-income households chosen by lottery from more than 176,000 applicants
result: No published evaluation yet

name: West Hollywood Pilot for Guaranteed Income
eligibility: West Hollywood residents (housed or unhoused) aged 50 and older with individual income of $41,400 or less; randomly selected
operator: City of West Hollywood with the National Council of Jewish Women, Los Angeles; evaluated by Penn's Center for Guaranteed Income Research
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 18 months (August 2022–January 2024) to 25 randomly selected low-income residents aged 50 and older
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Baltimore Young Families Success Fund
eligibility: Baltimore parents aged 18–24 with household income at or below 300% of the federal poverty level, chosen at random from more than 4,000 applicants; 130 recipients were in the study and 70 in a 'storytelling cohort', against 156 controls
operator: City of Baltimore under Mayor Brandon Scott, paid from $4.8 million of federal pandemic relief (ARPA) and foundation money, administered by the CASH Campaign of Maryland
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 24 months (August 2022–July 2024) to 200 young parents aged 18–24, chosen at random from more than 4,000 applicants
result: The final evaluation (October 2025), compared with 156 controls: 56% of recipients were food insecure at 18 months vs 72% of controls, and recipients missed about 9 fewer hours of work a month by the end. Abt Global's interim brief (June 2024) found 27% had applied to college or trade school at 12 months vs 13% of controls
evaluation.by: Abt Global (interim brief, June 2024); final report October 2025

name: Madison Forward Fund
eligibility: Madison residents 18+ with at least one child aged 17 or under, household income under 200% of the federal poverty line; chosen at random from about 3,000 applicants
operator: City of Madison, with payments funded entirely by private donors including Mayors for a Guaranteed Income and local foundations
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (September 2022–August 2023) to 155 low-income Madison households with children, chosen at random from about 3,000 applicants
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Austin Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Low-income Austin residents under an income cap who were exiting homelessness, facing eviction or at least two months behind on rent; enrolled through ten community organizations
operator: City of Austin with the nonprofit UpTogether, paid from $1.14 million of city money plus St. David's Foundation for 50 households
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 12 months (September 2022–August 2023) to 135 low-income households facing housing insecurity
result: The Urban Institute (2024) surveyed 54 of the 135 households: they spent about 60% of the money on rent or mortgage, 14% more caught up on housing payments and 12% fewer felt at risk of eviction; mental health improved at six months but was back near baseline at 12; no control group
evaluation.by: Urban Institute

name: Denver Basic Income Project
eligibility: Adults (aged 18–86) experiencing homelessness in Denver: on the streets, in shelters, in vehicles or on friends' couches
operator: The Denver Basic Income Project, a nonprofit, funded by foundations, donors and $2 million of the City of Denver's federal pandemic relief (ARPA) money
paid: $1,000 a month for a year (or $6,500 up front then $500 a month) with no conditions, from late 2022, to people experiencing homelessness in Denver; 807 enrolled across the two cash groups and a comparison group that got $50 a month
result: The University of Denver's year-one report (June 2024) reported that about 45% of participants across all three groups were renting or owning a home at 10 months, nights in shelters halved in the two cash groups, and full-time work rose in those groups while falling in the $50 group; stress was slightly higher at the end
evaluation.by: University of Denver Center for Housing and Homelessness Research

name: Silicon Valley Guaranteed Income Project
eligibility: Santa Clara County families with children under 18 who are homeless or at risk of losing their housing; by referral only (from the county housing waitlist and San Jose's Mayfair neighborhood)
operator: Destination: Home, a Silicon Valley nonprofit working on homelessness, with community partners and tech-industry and foundation donors
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for two years to 150 Santa Clara County families with children who were homeless or at risk of homelessness, starting in December 2022
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Elevate MV
eligibility: Mountain View residents (any immigration or housing status) with income at or below 30% of Area Median Income who are a parent or caregiver of a child under 18 (or pregnant); chosen at random
operator: City of Mountain View, run by the nonprofit Community Services Agency, with technical help from Mayors for a Guaranteed Income
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for two years (December 2022–November 2024) to 166 extremely low-income Mountain View families with children, chosen at random; 132 other applicants formed a control group
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Cook County Promise Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Cook County residents 18+, household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, not in another guaranteed income program; chosen by lottery in November 2022 from more than 233,000 applicants
operator: Cook County government (which includes Chicago), paid from $42 million of federal pandemic relief (ARPA); the University of Chicago Inclusive Economy Lab runs the evaluation
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for two years (December 2022–January 2025) to 3,250 low-to-moderate-income households chosen by lottery from more than 233,000 applicants
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Evanston Guaranteed Income Pilot Program
eligibility: Evanston residents at or below 250% of the federal poverty line who were aged 18–24, aged 62 or older, or undocumented, in equal numbers; chosen by lottery
operator: City of Evanston with Northwestern University, paid from the city's federal pandemic relief (ARPA) money, Northwestern and the Evanston Community Foundation
paid: $500 a month on a prepaid debit card with no conditions for 12 months (December 2022–November 2023) to 150 low-income young adults, seniors and undocumented residents chosen by lottery
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Rise Up Alameda
eligibility: Low-income households in the City of Alameda, chosen by lottery (average household income $31,836)
operator: City of Alameda, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for two years (2023–December 2025) to 150 low-income Alameda households chosen by lottery; 180 randomly selected applicants formed a control group
result: Abt Global's one-year interim report (2025) reported that, compared with the control group, fewer recipients were going into debt (15% vs 42%), more had money left at month's end (13% vs 1%) and nearly twice as many had $500+ saved, with lower stress; no negative effect on employment and no significant housing change
evaluation.by: Abt Global

name: Guaranteed Income for Artists (Springboard for the Arts)
city: Saint Paul and Otter Tail County
eligibility: Artists in Saint Paul and rural Otter Tail County (75 in the first group, 25 rural artists added in 2025)
place: Saint Paul and Otter Tail County, Minnesota, USA
operator: Springboard for the Arts, a Saint Paul arts nonprofit, paid for by private foundations
paid: $500 a month with no strings attached to 75 artists in Saint Paul and Otter Tail County from 2023, first for 18 months and then extended to five years ($30,000 each), with 25 more rural artists added in 2025 for 100 in total
result: No published evaluation yet

name: St. Louis Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot
eligibility: City residents with a child in St. Louis Public Schools or a public charter school, household income within poverty guidelines, with COVID-19 hardship; chosen by lottery from more than 5,000 applicants
operator: City of St. Louis (Treasurer's Office), paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA) and a $1 million gift from Jack Dorsey; donors finished it after a lawsuit froze public funds
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months (late 2023–May 2025, paused by a court order in July 2024) to 540 low-income families with school-age children, chosen by lottery from more than 5,000 applicants
result: Washington University's Brown School (December 2025) reported fewer missed rent and utility payments and less food insecurity (family surveys), and credit scores up 12 points on average versus similar St. Louis residents who were not paid (193 consented to credit tracking); not a randomized trial, and the 2024 payment pause coincided with a dip in credit health
evaluation.by: Washington University in St. Louis, Brown School (Center for Social Development and Evaluation Center; lead Stephen Roll)

name: New Haven guaranteed income pilot for formerly incarcerated people
eligibility: New Haven residents aged 25–55 released from prison within the past year
operator: The nonprofit 4-CT, with the City of New Haven and the Project M.O.R.E. reentry center
paid: $500 a month with no conditions on a prepaid card for a year to 20 people aged 25–55 recently released from prison, with reentry support
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Guaranteed Income for Trans People (GIFT)
eligibility: Transgender San Francisco residents 18+ with monthly income no higher than $600; random selection within priority categories (aim of at least 60% Black trans people; priority for monolingual Spanish speakers and undocumented people); no Social Security number needed
operator: City of San Francisco, run with Lyon-Martin Community Health Services (a clinic for trans, nonbinary and intersex people) and the Transgender District
paid: Up to $1,200 a month with no conditions for up to 18 months (January 2023–June 2024) to 55 low-income transgender residents, with optional gender-affirming health care, case management and financial coaching
result: No published evaluation yet

name: NET (Nourish, Empower, Trust) Growth Movement
eligibility: Young people who aged out of extended foster care supervised by Alameda County (67 of 90 eligible enrolled)
operator: Alameda County Social Services Agency, paid from county funds; designed by young people with experience of foster care
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 24 months (January 2023–December 2024) to 67 young people who had aged out of extended foster care, with optional case management and savings matches
result: Chapin Hall (January 2026, formative evaluation, self-reported; 26 and 23 survey respondents) reported that 73% were food insecure before the pilot, 27% while being paid and 44% in the six months after it ended. Economic hardships were also more common after payments stopped. No control group
evaluation.by: Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago (Amy Dworsky and Molly Van Drunen)

name: Pathway to Income Equity
eligibility: Sonoma County residents pregnant and/or parenting a child under 6, household income up to 185% of the federal poverty level ($51,338 for a family of four), with COVID-19 economic losses; picked at random from 2,383 eligible families out of 6,450 applications
operator: First 5 Sonoma County, a public early-childhood agency, with Sonoma County and several cities, mostly paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for two years, from February 2023, to 305 low-income Sonoma County families with a baby on the way or a child under 6, chosen at random from 2,383 eligible families
result: No published evaluation yet

name: ARISE (Alexandria Recurring Income for Success and Equity)
eligibility: Alexandria residents 18+ with income at or below 50% of area median income (about $64,050 for a family of three), chosen at random from 4,149 eligible applicants; 210 others formed a control group
operator: City of Alexandria (Department of Community and Human Services), paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA) and then city money, with a randomized evaluation by Abt Global
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 29 months (February 2023–June 2025, extended from 24) to 170 low-income residents chosen at random from 4,149 eligible applicants
result: Abt Global's final report (April 2026), compared with 210 controls: a statistically significant drop in homelessness by month 24, a significantly larger share able to cover costs and less use of payday loans, but no measurable gain in food security; changes in stress measures were modest
evaluation.by: Abt Global (Hannah Thomas, Meryl Finkel, AshLee Smith Playfair and others)

name: Family Income for Empowerment Program (FIEP)
eligibility: San Diego County families with a child under 18, income at or below 200% of the federal poverty line, referred by the county Child and Family Well-Being Department; random lottery prioritising 39 health-equity ZIP codes and unhoused families
operator: County of San Diego (Child and Family Well-Being Department), paid from federal pandemic relief and run by Jewish Family Service of San Diego
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 24 months, from March 2023, to 408 low-income families referred by the county child welfare department (up to 452 planned), aiming to keep children out of foster care
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Chicago Future Fund
eligibility: Formerly incarcerated people in the Austin, West Garfield Park and Englewood neighborhoods (round two)
operator: Equity and Transformation (EAT) Chicago, a nonprofit run by and for people affected by incarceration, with foundation support including the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (March 2023–February 2024) to 100 formerly incarcerated people in three West and South Side neighborhoods (the fund's second round)
result: An evaluation for EAT (report by Ashley Baber, published February 2025; 100 surveyed, 20 interviewed) reported late bill payments down 15 percentage points and homelessness in the prior month down 9 points from the start of the program, with 3 of 100 reporting recidivism; self-reported, with no control group
evaluation.by: Equity and Transformation (report by Ashley Baber), with Robert Wood Johnson Foundation support

name: Direct Cash Transfer Plus (DCT+)
eligibility: Young people aged 18–24 experiencing homelessness or unstable housing; the cash was not counted as income for other benefits
place: Oregon, USA (Multnomah, Clackamas and Deschutes counties)
operator: The Oregon Department of Human Services' Youth Experiencing Homelessness Program, paid from the state budget, with the nonprofit Point Source Youth and three local youth groups
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for two years (March 2023–March 2025), plus a one-time $3,000, to 120 homeless young people aged 18–24 in three Oregon counties, with optional housing and money-management support
result: Young People to the Front's final report (released January 2026) reported that 94% of the 63 youth who completed surveys said they were housed at the end, and 72% were working or in school; these are self-reported, with no control group and fewer than half the participants surveyed
evaluation.by: Young People to the Front

name: Long Beach Pledge Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Single-earner families with children under 18 at or below the federal poverty line; cohort 1 in ZIP code 90813, cohort 2 in ZIP codes 90802, 90804, 90805, 90806 and 90810; randomly selected
operator: City of Long Beach, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA) for the first cohort and city homelessness emergency funds for the second; the Fund for Guaranteed Income delivered payments
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months to 450 families with children below the poverty line, in two cohorts: 250 in ZIP code 90813 (May 2023–April 2024) and 200 in five other ZIP codes (March 2024–February 2025)
result: CSULB researchers (preliminary final report on cohort 1, September 2024) compared single-parent recipients with a randomly assigned control group: two months after payments ended, 44.6% vs 66.7% had cut meal sizes and 72.3% vs 50.0% had high-speed internet, with no significant effect on employment; self-reported surveys, 79 controls, 51–63% response
evaluation.by: California State University, Long Beach research team (Mileva, Steimetz, Woodward, Zentgraf)

name: Palm Springs Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Palm Springs residents earning under $16,600 a year who are past or present clients of DAP Health or Queer Works and agree to surveys; transgender and nonbinary people encouraged to apply but not required; chosen at random on March 30, 2023
operator: Two Palm Springs nonprofits, Queer Works and DAP Health, paid from city money; DAP Health took over in July 2024 after payment problems
paid: $800 a month with no conditions for 18 months, from May 2023, to 30 low-income residents who are clients of the two nonprofits, chosen at random; transgender and nonbinary people were encouraged to apply
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Rise Up Cambridge
eligibility: Cambridge families with children earning at or below 250% of the federal poverty level; open to all eligible families who applied
operator: City of Cambridge, a citywide follow-up to the RISE pilot paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 18 months from June 2023 to nearly 2,000 low-income families with children (at or below 250% of the federal poverty level)
result: MDRC (April 2026), from surveys and interviews with no control group: 93% of survey respondents used the money for food and 75% for emergencies, and 96% reported less stress while paid. For nearly half, the $500 plus household income still fell below the federal poverty line
evaluation.by: MDRC (Mina Addo, lead author)

name: Quality Housing Coalition cash pilot for single mothers
eligibility: Low-income single mothers, many previously homeless and mostly asylum seekers and refugees
operator: Quality Housing Coalition, a Portland nonprofit, paid from private donations and grants
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for a year from June 2023 to 20 low-income single mothers, alongside social support; a second group of 20 began in September 2024
result: The coalition's own study (September 2024), as reported by the Bangor Daily News, compared with a control group: the number saying they were doing OK or better financially rose from one to about half, while the control group stayed flat, and all participants stayed housed. Very small sample (n = 20)
evaluation.by: Quality Housing Coalition (own study, reported by the Bangor Daily News)

name: GROW (Guaranteed Resources Optimize Wellbeing) Study
eligibility: Parents on Extended TANF (cash aid after the 60-month limit) enrolled in the city's Work Ready program; randomized, with 239 controls getting $50 a month
operator: City of Philadelphia's Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity, paid from existing Extended TANF funds (about $322,000), with payments delivered by the Fund for Guaranteed Income
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months from June 2023 to 51 parents on Extended TANF, while 239 others in a randomized control group got $50 a month
result: Reinvestment Fund and University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee researchers (May 2026), compared with the $50 control group: modest but statistically significant gains in financial wellbeing, mental health and food insecurity, which returned to baseline or slightly worse after payments stopped. Small sample (51)
evaluation.by: Reinvestment Fund and University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (David Pate Jr.)

name: United Way Guaranteed Income Program, City of Sacramento cohort
eligibility: City of Sacramento residents with income below 150% of the California Poverty Measure; picked at random from nearly 13,000 applicants
operator: United Way California Capital Region, paid from the City of Sacramento's federal pandemic relief (ARPA)
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for one year (July 2023–June 2024) to 80 low-income Sacramento households picked at random from nearly 13,000 applicants
result: Sacramento State (2025) reported that, by the end, 46% of recipients said they were financially better off vs 19% of the control group; 13% got an eviction or pay-rent notice vs 24%; recipients' food insecurity fell from 51% to 37%. Six months after payments ended, 41% vs 10% still felt better off. Self-reported
evaluation.by: Sacramento State University School of Social Work (Ethan Evans and colleagues)

name: El Monte Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: El Monte single mothers (female head of household, no spouse or partner) with children under 18, income at or below the poverty line, hit financially by COVID-19; chosen from more than 2,500 applications
operator: City of El Monte, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA); the RAND Corporation ran enrollment and the evaluation with USC
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for a year (first payment July 2023, last scheduled May 31, 2024) to 125 low-income single mothers chosen from more than 2,500 applications
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Rochester Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot
eligibility: Low-income Rochester residents, chosen at random from 11,698 eligible applicants in two cohorts (175 paid September 2023–August 2024, 176 paid December 2023–November 2024)
operator: City of Rochester, paid largely from federal COVID relief money, with a randomized study by Notre Dame's Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months to 351 low-income residents picked at random from 11,698 eligible applicants, in two cohorts paid between September 2023 and November 2024
result: Notre Dame researchers (reported December 2025), compared with applicants not selected: recipients were nearly three times as likely to have improved savings, 51% less likely to expect material hardship and 25% more likely to be driving a car at the end, with no difference in paying off past debt. Surveyed at the last payment, so no long-term effects; described as modest
evaluation.by: University of Notre Dame, Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities (Patrick Turner and colleagues)

name: San Francisco Guaranteed Income Pilot for Young People Who Aged Out of Extended Foster Care
eligibility: Young people who aged out of extended foster care in San Francisco
operator: San Francisco Human Services Agency, with a state grant from the California Department of Social Services, the first state-funded guaranteed income program in the US
paid: $1,200 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 150 former foster youth in San Francisco, starting in October 2023
result: No published evaluation yet

name: VC Thrive Supplemental Income Pilot
eligibility: Former foster youth aged 21–26 who aged out of care in Ventura County, under HUD low-income limits
operator: Ventura County Human Services Agency, one of California's first state-funded guaranteed income pilots, with county matching money; James Storehouse made the payments
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 18 months, from October 2023, to 150 former foster youth aged 21–26 who aged out of care in Ventura County
result: No published evaluation yet

name: California Guaranteed Income Pilot for Former Foster Youth (iFoster, statewide)
eligibility: Young people leaving extended foster care in California, outside the counties that ran their own state-funded pilots
operator: iFoster, a national nonprofit for foster youth, with a grant from the California Department of Social Services
paid: $750 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 354 young people leaving foster care across California, starting in November 2023
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Rx Kids
eligibility: Every expectant mother in a participating community, with no income test; enrol from 16+ weeks of pregnancy until the baby is six months old
place: Flint, Michigan, USA (since expanded to about 42 Michigan communities, including Detroit)
operator: Michigan State University, with GiveDirectly delivering the money, funded by the State of Michigan and private donors
paid: $1,500 during pregnancy and then $500 a month for the baby's first year, with no conditions or income test, to every mother in Flint from 2024; by May 2026 it had reached more than 11,000 families in 42 Michigan communities
result: A Lancet Public Health study (May 2026; about 4,500 Flint births, 2021–mid-2025, compared with similar Michigan cities) estimated 18% fewer preterm births, 27% less low birthweight and about 29% fewer NICU admissions after the 2024 launch; quasi-experimental, by researchers from the program's own universities
evaluation.by: Michigan State University and University of Michigan researchers

name: In Her Hands (second cohort, Atlanta's west side)
eligibility: Women on Atlanta's west side (Vine City and English Avenue); other criteria not stated in the sources read
place: Atlanta (Vine City and English Avenue), Georgia, USA
operator: Georgia Resilience and Opportunity Fund (GRO Fund), expanded with a $6.2 million grant from the Arthur M. Blank Family Foundation
paid: An average of $1,000 a month with no conditions for 36 months from 2024 to 270 women on Atlanta's west side, with the option of a smaller monthly amount plus a lump sum
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Humboldt Income Program
eligibility: Humboldt County residents 18+, under 28 weeks pregnant at enrollment, income at or below 200% of the federal poverty level, referred by a partner health or social service agency; randomly assigned to $920 or to a $20-a-month control group
operator: McKinleyville Family Resource Center, a nonprofit, with a California state grant and local donations
paid: $920 a month with no conditions for 18 months to 150 low-income pregnant people in Humboldt County, from January 2024; another 100 applicants were randomly assigned to get $20 a month as a control group
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Inland SoCal United Way Guaranteed Income Pilot
eligibility: Pregnant people 18+ in Riverside County, within the first six months of pregnancy at application, household income under $90,616 a year, referred by partner agencies; plus former foster youth in Riverside and San Bernardino counties
place: Riverside and San Bernardino counties, California, USA
operator: Inland Southern California United Way, the largest of California's seven state-funded guaranteed income pilots, with county and foundation money
paid: $600 a month with no conditions for 12 months, from January 2024, to 409 pregnant people in Riverside County, plus $750 a month for 18 months to 35 former foster youth in Riverside and San Bernardino counties
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Guaranteed Income to Grow Ann Arbor (GIG A2)
eligibility: Ann Arbor residents with household income at or below 225% of the federal poverty line who do gig work, informal or small business; randomly selected from over 1,000 applicants
operator: City of Ann Arbor, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA); the University of Michigan's Poverty Solutions ran and evaluated it
paid: $528 a month with no conditions for two years (January 2024–December 2025) to 100 low-income entrepreneurs and gig workers chosen at random from over 1,000 applicants; another 100 got $25 a month as a comparison group
result: U-M Poverty Solutions' Year 1 report (January 2026, 100 recipients vs 100 comparison) found no statistically significant differences in food, housing or utility insecurity after one year; both groups had food insecurity of 58–61%. Recipients said they spent mostly on food (68%) and household supplies (60%), and interviewees described less stress. Preliminary; final report due in 2026
evaluation.by: Poverty Solutions, University of Michigan

name: Elevate Boulder
eligibility: Low-income Boulder households (detailed criteria not on fetched pages)
operator: The City of Boulder, paid mainly from federal pandemic relief (ARPA), with help from the Community Foundation Boulder County and private donors
paid: $500 a month with no strings attached for two years (from January 2024) to 200 low-income Boulder households
result: An evaluation by the Omni Institute (September 2025, first 20 months, surveys of participants before and during the program) reported significantly less psychological distress and food insecurity and easier rent and utility payments; there was no significant change in employment, savings, debt or the ability to cover a $400 expense, and there was no control group
evaluation.by: Center for Social Investment, Omni Institute

name: Pregnancy Assistance Income with Dignity (P.A.I.D.)
eligibility: Pregnant people 18+ in their first or second trimester (before week 27) at enrollment, living in Los Angeles County, household income at or below HUD's low-income limit; randomly selected
operator: National Council of Jewish Women, Los Angeles, with a grant from California's state-funded guaranteed income pilot program
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 18 months, from April 2024, to 180 randomly selected low-income pregnant people in Los Angeles County
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Thrive Prince George's
eligibility: 125 seniors aged 60+ and 50 young people aged 18–24 who aged out of foster care, in high-poverty zip codes with income above the poverty line but below the cost of living (ALICE)
operator: Greater Washington Community Foundation, with funding from Prince George's County and the Meyer Foundation
paid: $800 a month with no conditions for 24 months from April 2024 to 175 people: 125 low-income seniors and 50 young adults who aged out of foster care
result: No published evaluation yet

name: The Bridge Project in Milwaukee
eligibility: Pregnant women 18+, 23 weeks pregnant or less, in ZIP codes 53204, 53205, 53206 or 53215, household income under $39,000; chosen by lottery
operator: The Bridge Project, a New York-born nonprofit program, with Milwaukee's Zilber Family Foundation and later public money
paid: $1,125 before birth, then $750 a month for 15 months and $375 a month for 21 months (three years in all) with no strings attached, from June 2024, to 122 low-income pregnant women in four Milwaukee ZIP codes chosen by lottery
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Advancing Fresno County Guaranteed Income
eligibility: Parents or caregivers who are pregnant or have a child aged 0–5, living in ZIP 93706 (southwest Fresno) or 93234 (Huron), income at or below 80% of the local Area Median Income; 75 picked by lottery in each area from about 10,000 applications
place: Fresno and Huron, Fresno County, California, USA
operator: Fresno Economic Opportunities Commission, a local anti-poverty agency, paid for by private foundations
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months (July 2024–June 2025) to 150 low-income families with young children, 75 in southwest Fresno and 75 in rural Huron, chosen by lottery
result: Fresno State's Center for Community Voices (December 2025; randomized trial with 300 families) reported that borrowing for regular expenses fell from 40% to 18%, along with less food insecurity and parental stress, and no significant effect on employment
evaluation.by: Center for Community Voices, Fresno State (led by Amber Crowell)

name: Somerville Guaranteed Basic Income Pilot
eligibility: Somerville households at high risk of housing insecurity and displacement, identified from existing city and school caseloads
operator: City of Somerville, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA), evaluated by UMass Boston's Collins Center
paid: $750 a month with no conditions on a reloadable debit card for 12 months (July 2024–June 2025) to 198 households at high risk of losing their housing
result: UMass Boston's Collins Center (2026), comparing participants before and after with no control group: the share who rarely or never had money left at month's end fell from 73% to 55%, and 66% of the 33 households behind on rent caught up. Self-reported
evaluation.by: Edward J. Collins Center for Public Management, UMass Boston

name: UpTogether Illinois guaranteed income pilot
city: Peoria, Rockford and other Illinois cities
eligibility: Families earning up to 80% of the area median income in nine Illinois cities
place: Downstate Illinois (Peoria, Carbondale, Springfield, Bloomington, Normal, Champaign, Rockford, Belleville and East St. Louis), USA
operator: UpTogether, a national nonprofit, paid for by a private donor, to build the case for a statewide program
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for one year from September 2024 to 52 families in nine downstate Illinois cities, including Peoria and Rockford
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Nurturing Futures
eligibility: Boulder County residents 18+ with at least one child under 4 and family income below 30% of area median income; chosen by lottery in September 2024
operator: Boulder County's Department of Human Services, paid from federal pandemic relief (ARPA), with AidKit helping with applications
paid: $300 a month with no spending restrictions for two years, from October 2024, to 725 Boulder County households with a child under 4 and income below 30% of the area median, chosen by lottery; in May 2026 the county voted to continue it at $600 a month
result: No published evaluation yet

name: BOOST (Building Outstanding Opportunities for Students to Thrive)
eligibility: LACCD students at East LA, LA City, LA Trade-Technical or LA Southwest colleges, with 12+ units completed and 6+ current units, in or interested in health careers, with financial need
operator: Los Angeles Community College District, paid with private money from the Broad Foundation and the California Community Foundation's Young Adults Forward Fund
paid: $1,000 a month with no conditions for 12 months (November 2024–October 2025) to 251 low-income community college students in health-career programs; over 300 others formed a comparison group
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Ohio Mothers Trust
eligibility: Single mothers in Columbus with incomes at or below 80% of area median income, selected by the Motherful collective
operator: Three nonprofits (RISE Together Innovation Institute, Motherful and UpTogether), paid with $211,200 of their own and donor money
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for 12 months from December 2024 to 32 single mothers in Columbus
result: No published evaluation yet

name: Uplift Salem
eligibility: Salem residents with household income at or below 100% of the federal poverty level, chosen by lottery; 100 others formed a comparison group
operator: City of Salem with the nonprofit UpTogether, paid from federal COVID relief and private money, studied by Salem State University
paid: $500 a month with no conditions for a year (December 2024–November 2025) to 100 residents living at or below the poverty line, chosen by lottery
result: Salem State University researchers' preliminary findings (March 2026), self-reported by participants: 37% strongly agreed they were better prepared for unexpected challenges at the end, up 10 points from August, and about three-quarters of parents spent more time with their children. A final report was due later
evaluation.by: Salem State University, North Shore Policy Lab

name: The Bridge Project (Appalachia)
city: Appalachian Ohio, Kentucky and West Virginia
eligibility: Pregnant women aged 18+, 23 weeks or fewer into pregnancy, household income $44,000 or less, living within the Appalachian Regional Commission area in Ohio, Kentucky or West Virginia; chosen by lottery
place: Appalachian Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia, USA
operator: The Bridge Project, started by the New York-based Monarch Foundation
paid: $1,125 during pregnancy, then $750 a month for 15 months and $375 a month for 21 months with no conditions, from April 2025, to 500 low-income mothers in Appalachian Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia; 750 others get small payments for surveys
result: No published evaluation yet

name: IndyEast Guaranteed Income Initiative
eligibility: Invitation only: randomly selected from neighbors already receiving coaching or case management at one of the three partner centers on Indianapolis's east side
operator: Three east-side Indianapolis community centers, funded by a $2.5 million United Way of Central Indiana grant
paid: $500 a month for 18 months from October 2025, with optional coaching, to 25 east-side households picked at random from the centers' clients; the goal is 125 households by 2026
result: No published evaluation yet

name: ROOTED (Resources & Opportunities for Ongoing Transition, Empowerment & Dignity)
eligibility: Durham residents released after 1 January 2024 after at least nine consecutive months of incarceration, with income at or below 60% of area median income; chosen by lottery
operator: City of Durham (Community Safety Department), with $1 million from the city council after the Excel pilot; evaluated by Duke University researchers
paid: $8,400 over a year with no conditions ($700 a month, or larger early payments that taper) in 2026 to 107 formerly incarcerated Durham residents chosen by lottery; unselected applicants form the comparison group
result: No published evaluation yet

name: AI Dividend
eligibility: Workers whose pay, jobs or opportunities were harmed by AI (not only tech workers: call-center workers, copywriters, journalists, data annotators, creative and other knowledge workers); applicants complete a survey, the AI Commons Project checks eligibility, and people are selected on a rolling basis
place: Run by US nonprofits, for people whose work has been hurt by AI
operator: What We Will (an advocacy group for AI-affected workers) and the AI Commons Project, part of the Fund for Guaranteed Income, which funds it
paid: $1,000 a month with no strings attached for a year, alongside reskilling, to a first cohort of 25–50 workers hurt by AI, selected on a rolling basis; the first payments went out in March 2026
result: No published evaluation yet
